When someone asks you a question you did not prepare for, your brain wants to do two things: panic, or talk too much. Here is a better plan. First, buy time honestly. Say: that is a good question, let me think for a second. Three seconds of silence sound confident, not lost. Second, tell people how sure you are. If you are almost certain, use must: it must be the old data. If you are not sure, use might or could: it might be the timing. And if something is impossible, use can't: that can't be right, we checked it twice. Third, make one point, give one reason, and stop. Rambling is the real enemy. Nobody remembers your fifth sentence, but everybody remembers if you had a clear first one.

Hi Carlos, Mark Ellison here. Just a quick heads-up for tomorrow's leadership offsite. Our new CFO will be in the room. She must have read the post-mortem, because she asked me about it this morning. She might ask you about the final cost of the bridge, and she could ask about the next integration, too. Do not worry about exact numbers. A ballpark figure is fine, and if you do not know, an educated guess is better than silence. One more thing: the session starts at nine and there are twelve people on the list, so the questions will come fast. Keep your answers short. See you tomorrow.
